Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) specifically applies to "a surviving spouse (as defined in section 2(a))". Alice and Bob are married (they married on Feb 3, 2017) and file a joint return, not a surviving spouse situation. Section 63(c)(2)(A)(i) would apply to their joint return, but Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) does not apply since Alice is not a surviving spouse.
reasoning:
Let me analyze this carefully.

The question is asking whether Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) applies to Alice in 2017.

Looking at the statute, Section 63(c)(2) defines the basic standard deduction:

"(2) Basic standard deduction
For purposes of paragraph (1), the basic standard deduction is-
(A) 200 percent of the dollar amount in effect under subparagraph (C) for the taxable year in the case of-
(i) a joint return, or
(ii) a surviving spouse (as defined in section 2(a)),
(B) $4,400 in the case of a head of household (as defined in section 2(b)), or
(C) $3,000 in any other case."

So Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) refers to "a surviving spouse (as defined in section 2(a))"

The question states:
- Alice was paid $33,200 in 2017
- Alice and Bob have been married since Feb 3rd, 2017
- They file a joint return for 2017

The question asks whether Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) applies to Alice.

Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) specifically mentions "a surviving spouse (as defined in section 2(a))".

Alice and Bob are married (not survived by a spouse), and they file a joint return. Section 63(c)(2)(A)(i) applies to "a joint return" which is what Alice is filing.

So Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) specifically applies to surviving spouses, not to individuals filing joint returns as married couples.

The claim is "Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) applies to Alice in 2017."

This would be a Contradiction because:
1. Alice is married, not a surviving spouse
2. She files a joint return, which falls under Section 63(c)(2)(A)(i), not (A)(ii)


3. Section 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) is specifically for surviving spouses, not married filing jointly

The answer is Contradiction.
